text: A typical web request is fast, so scaling by adding instances smooths out load reasonably well. An AI inference request can take seconds to tens of seconds -- holding a connection open that whole time doesn't scale the same way.

A synchronous request holds the client's connection open the entire time. An asynchronous request returns a job ID immediately, a worker picks it up when free, and the client polls or gets a webhook for the result later.

With autoscaling alone, a burst needs more instances right now, and GPU instances start in minutes. A queue in front of autoscaling lets requests wait briefly while instances catch up -- nothing gets rejected, just delayed.

A failing job gets retried a few times and then moved to a dead-letter queue instead of blocking everything behind it. Without one, a single poison-pill request can consume retry attempts and worker capacity forever.

A queue turns an instant-reaction problem into a catch-up-eventually problem, which matters enormously given how slow a GPU cold start actually is. Next up: putting a dollar figure on everything this chapter has covered -- cost-aware scaling.
